cita: Ren et al. (2026). MemLens: Benchmarking Multimodal Long-Term Memory in Large Vision-Language Models.
problema: Argues no existing benchmark length-controls a head-to-head comparison of long-context LVLMs vs memory-augmented agents on multimodal questions that genuinely require visual (not just textual) evidence, since prior multimodal conversational benchmarks (e.g. LoCoMo) admit text-only shortcuts.
mecanismo: Not a memory mechanism (operaciones/representacion=NA): MEMLENS is a benchmark-construction pipeline - hierarchical-topic session simulation (dual-LLM user/assistant dialogue with selected images), entity-abstraction question generation that forces cross-modal dependency (named entity replaced by an image reference), evidence sessions stylistically matched to distractors, and timestamp-ordered assembly into four standardized context lengths (32K-256K) under a cross-modal token-counting scheme, covering five memory abilities (extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, refusal).
evaluacion: Evaluated 27 LVLMs (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.5, GLM-4.6V, Gemma3, etc.) and 7 memory-augmented agents (M3-Agent, M2A, M3C, Mem0, MemOS, MemAgent-7B, Memory-T1) across four context lengths with LLM-as-Judge accuracy (cross-validated kappa=0.93 vs human consensus); ran an image-ablation study on 634 image-essential/-supportive questions to validate that visual evidence is genuinely required.
numeros_clave: Image-ablation: removing evidence images drops GPT-5.4 from 93.13% to 1.74% and Gemini-3.1-Pro from 89.42% to 1.89% overall accuracy (Table 3, roughly -90pp); Multi-Session Reasoning caps most systems below 30% (ceiling 44.06% at 32K); best LVLM Gemini-3.1-Pro degrades only 2.11pp from 32K to 128K (54.1% -> 52.0%) while several open-weight leaders lose more than 13pp (Fig 2).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Systematically measures retrieval quality across context lengths and 34 systems rather than trusting any single reported number (Fig 2, Table 3 ablation), directly modeling the measured-retrieval discipline MF's G-M2 calls for.

Its Knowledge-Update task (track an evolving attribute across 4 successive updates, answer from the final state) is a staleness-handling stress test, but as a benchmark rather than a mechanism it only indirectly informs MF's own anti-drift design (Sec 3.1).

notes: Table 1-3, Fig 2, Sec 3.4 cross-modality validation (arXiv:2605.14906v1); a benchmark/dataset paper (operaciones/representacion=NA), not a memory architecture itself.

cita: Chai et al. (2026). SMMBench: A Benchmark for Source-Distributed Multimodal Agent Memory.
problema: Identifies source-distributed memory composition (evidence fragmented across independently-originated heterogeneous sources - chats, profiles, tables, screenshots, documents - none individually sufficient) as an under-evaluated bottleneck distinct from ordinary long-context reasoning, since prior benchmarks mostly test recall within one pre-assembled/coherent context.
mecanismo: Not a memory architecture (operaciones/representacion=NA): SMMBench is a benchmark-construction pipeline - QA preparation from public multimodal benchmarks, synthesis of multiple parallel conversational sources (group/private chats with recurring participants), then an LLM-based source-aware inserter that routes each evidence unit to a distinct source/position (preserving temporal consistency for conflicting/updated facts) so that at least 2 independent sources are required per answer; evaluated agents ingest the merged, timestamp-ordered observation stream into their own memory-update operator and must retrieve and compose across source boundaries.
evaluacion: 1877 QA samples over 264 sources, 5 task types (single-hop QA, multi-hop QA, conflict resolution, preference reasoning, function-call action prediction); benchmarked memory-style (MemGPT, MIRIX, Mem0, MemVerse, OmniSimpleMem, etc.) and RAG-style (NativeRAG, HMRAG, UniversalRAG, VRAG) baselines against Random and Golden-Evidence reference baselines, plus controlled ablations varying source-concentrated vs source-distributed placement and the number of required sources.
numeros_clave: Best system overall score 0.4933 (MIRIX, native multimodal) vs Golden-Evidence-Baseline 0.7473 and Random-Baseline 0.2000 (Table 3); Function-Call is hardest (best score 0.1111, Golden-Evidence only 0.2778); MIRIX improves 0.2496->0.3161 overall moving from Text+Caption to native multimodal while MemGPT drops 0.3708->0.2713 on the same move, showing native multimodal access alone doesn't fix source-distributed composition.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Empirically shows that composing a fact from >=2 independently-originated sources (no single source sufficient) is a major, still-unsolved bottleneck even for mature memory systems (Table 3), supporting MF's single-source-per-fact/seams concern rather than assuming multi-store composition is solved.

Its Conflict-Resolution task (outdated evidence in one source must be overridden by newer evidence in another, with enforced temporal-dependency consistency at construction time, Sec 3.2) is a concrete cross-source staleness stress test MF could adapt for its own multi-doc drift checks.

notes: Table 1-3, Fig 4-5, Sec 3.1-3.3 construction pipeline (arXiv:2605.15710v1); a benchmark/dataset paper (operaciones/representacion=NA), not a memory architecture itself.

cita: Tao et al. (2026). MemConflict: Evaluating Long-Term Memory Systems Under Memory Conflicts.
problema: Argues that existing long-term memory evaluations mostly measure outcome-level QA/update performance without diagnosing whether systems retrieve and rank the temporally-valid, factually-correct, contextually-applicable memory item when multiple plausible/contradictory candidates compete (only 'dynamic'/update conflicts are typically covered by prior benchmarks).
mecanismo: Not a memory mechanism (operaciones/representacion=NA): MemConflict is a diagnostic benchmark-construction pipeline built from structured user profiles - it simulates a session timeline and deliberately inserts dynamic conflicts (true state updates), static conflicts (contradictory-but-false mentions that should NOT overwrite a stable fact), conditional conflicts (multiple values valid only under different query conditions), and semantically-similar distractors, then generates dialogues/queries/gold labels; evaluated memory systems are scored both black-box (answer accuracy, update-order-consistency, conflict-recognition) and white-box (whether/how highly the gold supporting memory is retrieved and ranked).
evaluacion: Evaluated six memory systems (A-Mem, LangMem, Letta, MemOS, Mem0, Memobase) with a two-level black-box+white-box protocol across dynamic/static/conditional conflict types, plus sensitivity analyses varying dialogue length, distractor injection, query formulation (direct vs implicit) and conflict distance (sessions between competing candidates).
numeros_clave: Black-box Answer Accuracy varies sharply by conflict type and system: MemOS best-average (0.5539) with static AA 0.4375 and conditional AA 0.8449, LangMem best on dynamic (0.4966) but worst on conditional (0.1556); static conflicts are hardest overall (all systems <=0.4375 AA) while conditional conflicts are easiest but most polarized (Table 3); sensitivity analyses show longer histories, distractors, implicit queries and larger conflict distance all degrade performance (Sec 4).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Measures that 'static conflicts' (a later false/contradictory mention that should NOT overwrite a stable true fact) are the hardest conflict type for every evaluated system (Table 3, all AA<=0.4375), evidencing that naive recency-wins overwriting is unsafe and staleness/poisoning-resistance needs explicit handling, as MF's FIDELIDAD anchor assumes.

Its white-box protocol separates 'did the system answer correctly' from 'did it retrieve/rank the actual gold supporting memory' (Sec 3.6), operationalizing exactly the measured-retrieval discipline (not just outcome accuracy) that G-M2 calls for.

notes: Table 1 (framework comparison), Table 3 (main results), Sec 3-4 conflict-construction pipeline (arXiv:2605.20926v1); a benchmark/diagnostic-framework paper (operaciones/representacion=NA), not a memory architecture itself.

cita: Joshi (2026). Eywa: Provenance-Grounded Long-Term Memory for AI Agents.
problema: Targets that memory-backed answer failures are hard to diagnose because existing systems collapse source evidence, extracted facts, retrieved context, and answer policy into one opaque prompt path, so a wrong answer cannot be attributed to missing evidence, unsupported extraction, staleness, retrieval loss, or answer-model behavior.
mecanismo: Eywa's write path is two-tiered: Tier 0 immutably captures raw evidence plus deterministic typed-signal detection (dates, entities, amounts, IDs, no LLM call), then Tier 1 (ADMISION) has an LLM propose candidate facts that must pass a validator (source-overlap, hard-anchor match, subject match, negation/uncertainty preservation) before being written (WRITE) as canonical beliefs still linked via a provenance edge to their source evidence; beliefs are revisable/supersedable (ACTUALIZACION) and evidence is user-scope deletable (OLVIDO); retrieval is a deterministic, LLM-free multi-route read (temporal metadata, entity scope, keyword, vector similarity) returned separately from the answer-model's instructions, and an explicit 8-mode failure taxonomy (coverage/grounding/revision/scope/temporal/retrieval/synthesis/measurement gap) attributes each wrong answer to a specific layer.
evaluacion: Evaluated under a frozen, artifact-recorded retrieval configuration on LoCoMo C1-C4 (judge accuracy, Claude Sonnet 4.6 write+QA roles), LongMemEval-S (retrieval-sufficiency accuracy), and BEAM (700-question technical-memory stress benchmark, nugget score + pass@score>=0.5), reporting each benchmark under its own protocol with full per-question artifacts published for independent inspection; a 143-sample write-path audit directly checks validator behavior.
numeros_clave: 90.19% judge accuracy on LoCoMo C1-C4; 88.2% retrieval-sufficiency accuracy on LongMemEval-S; 81.45% mean nugget score / 85.29% pass@score>=0.5 on BEAM (700 questions); write-path audit: 67.4% of 143 candidate facts had no hard anchor (still checked by support/subject/polarity rules), validator rejected 11/132 candidates mainly for insufficient source overlap or invented hard values (Sec 1, Sec 4.1).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Enforces 'evidence before belief' as a single-source-of-truth invariant - extracted facts are a revisable INDEX over immutable evidence, never a lossy replacement (Sec 4.2) - directly confirming MF's single-source-per-fact seam over collapsing evidence+derived-fact+retrieval into one opaque store.

Its 8-mode failure taxonomy (coverage/grounding/revision/scope/temporal/retrieval/synthesis/measurement gap, Table 1) is a directly reusable vocabulary MF could adopt to classify WHY a memory answer was wrong, beyond a single pass/fail signal.

notes: Sec 1 (headline numbers), Sec 4.1 (write-path audit), Table 1-2 (failure taxonomy and object model) (arXiv:2605.30771v1). RECONSIDERAR - solo-author/company research note, self-reported evaluation with published per-question artifacts but no independent third-party replication found.

cita: Yang et al. (2026). RaMem: Contextual Reinstatement for Long-term Agentic Memory.
problema: Targets 'context collapse': existing memory systems compress experiences into decontextualized fragments that appear equally relevant to a query if they share entities/topics, so a retriever surfaces related-but-wrong-episode memories as if they were valid evidence, an evidence-misidentification failure distinct from a plain retrieval miss.
mecanismo: RaMem WRITEs each memory as content plus an episodic-context tuple (event time, mention time, session span, participants, location, entities, topic); at query time it induces a recall-condition frame from the query (grounded time/participants/entities), then does validity-aware retrieval that prioritizes session-overlap-compatible candidates while keeping content-only matches as fallback (falling back to plain content retrieval when recall conditions can't be grounded), and finally passes the selected memories to the generator with their structured episodic context intact rather than flattened text.
evaluacion: Evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval (SimpleMem protocol) across four backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B) with F1/BLEU-1 against LoCoMo-baseline, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-Mem, LightMem, Mem0 and SimpleMem; plus retrieval diagnostics (Recall@k, MRR, capped rank) using verified ground-truth memories, a dedicated context-collapse analysis (context-distractor rank), and a context-shuffle ablation that scrambles episodic-context fields while keeping content fixed.
numeros_clave: Average LoCoMo F1 improves over best baseline SimpleMem on all backbones (e.g. GPT-4o 51.66 vs 39.06, GPT-4.1-mini 54.23 vs 43.24); on GPT-4.1-mini Recall@10 rises 0.7221->0.7890 and MRR 0.4908->0.5476; SimpleMem ranks a context-distractor first in 43.66-54.14% of context-confusable examples, RaMem lowers this to 0.3495-0.4796 (Table 1-2, Fig 3); shuffling episodic-context fields (content unchanged) degrades GT Recall@10 from 0.7550 to ~0.66 (Table 3), confirming the gain comes from context binding, not extra text.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Formalizes an episodic-context provenance tuple (event time vs mention time vs session span, participants, location) attached to every memory and a validity check before using it as evidence (Sec 3.1-3.3), a concrete anti-drift pattern MF could adopt so a related-but-wrong-version doc isn't treated as current truth.

The context-shuffle ablation (Table 3) isolates that measured retrieval gains come specifically from correct content-context binding, not just extra metadata volume, a rigorous measured-retrieval methodology consistent with MF's G-M2 stance.

notes: Table 1-3, Fig 3, Sec 3.1-3.4 mechanism and ablations (arXiv:2606.22844v1).

cita: Xie et al. (2026). ECHO: Prune to Act, Trace to Learn with Selective Turn Memory in Agentic RL.
problema: Targets a coupled failure in long-horizon agentic RL: context managers that summarize/collapse distant history make long rollouts feasible for acting, but once original turns are no longer source-addressable, outcome-based RL loses an explicit way to route sparse final-answer credit back to the specific evidence turns that supported a correct answer (dense token-level credit reinforces redundant search along with useful evidence).
mecanismo: After each completed tool-use turn, ECHO WRITEs a compact memory record (source-turn index plus local finding, ADMISION into a non-collapsing memory set, never folded into one summary); at each compression boundary the policy itself selects a bounded subset of useful historical memories (autoregressive memory-selection action) to reconstruct the next bounded policy context (recent turns plus selected memories); the same selected source indices are then reused at training time as a provenance-guided credit mask, routing positive outcome advantage only to the final-answer segment, the selected source turns and their findings, and the memory-selection actions themselves (not every generated token).
evaluacion: Evaluated on BrowseComp-Plus (long-horizon tool-use QA, 747 train / 83 held-out) with Qwen3-32B-Instruct and transfer to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (MoE), comparing GRPO, SUPO rolling-summarization, and ECHO under the same tool environment/verifier; tracked held-out accuracy alongside turns-per-rollout, response length, generation time and trajectory volume over training, plus an ablation removing the traceable credit assignment (dense all-token credit).
numeros_clave: ECHO reaches 43.4% held-out accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus vs GRPO 28.9% and rolling-summary SUPO 36.1%, while using fewer turns and lower trajectory volume than SUPO (Abstract, Fig 1); SUPO shows turn proliferation and rising generation time/trajectory volume over training (Fig 2) that ECHO avoids.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Measures that collapsing history into rolling summaries to save context degrades training efficiency (turn proliferation, rising trajectory volume/generation time, Fig 2) versus selective non-collapsing memory, directly relevant to MF's context-economy anchor when choosing between summarization and selective retention.

Keeps every memory record linked to its original source turn, never collapsed into an untraceable summary (Sec 4.2), a provenance-preservation pattern MF could reuse so a derived/cached fact stays traceable back to its source doc.

The selection instruction can ask the policy to record 'planned next actions' among the reusable memories it keeps (Sec 4.2), a lightweight plan-state signal, but this is incidental to the paper's main RL-credit-assignment contribution rather than a dedicated plan-state mechanism (plan_estado=SI).
